{"id": "4:113/q16", "question": "What is the Book sent to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether 'Book' is identified by its text, its adjudicating function, or an inward form of knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q16/p1", "position": "The Quran or recited scripture.", "reasons": "Tabari says it contains clarification, guidance and admonition; Ibn Atiyya calls it recited revelation; Elmalili says it is proof above other proofs; Kuranyolu says its identification is unanimous."}, {"id": "4:113/q16/p2", "position": "It is revelation sent to settle people's disagreements.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 2:213 for this function."}, {"id": "4:113/q16/p3", "position": "It denotes comprehensive detailed knowledge after gifted existence.", "reasons": "Qashani gives the inward interpretation."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q17", "question": "What does Wisdom designate in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether Wisdom is the Prophet's Sunna, Quranic judgment and rulings, a faculty, prophethood, or other divine teaching.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q17/p1", "position": "Judgment by revelation, its rulings, or its lawful and forbidden commands.", "reasons": "Muqatil says lawful and unlawful; Tabari expands to commands, prohibitions, promises and warnings and compares 2:129; Abu Sulayman adds clarification, inspiration and a sound answer in the heart; Biqai sees grasp of the Book's purposes and sound practice; Study Quran has religious understanding more broadly."}, {"id": "4:113/q17/p2", "position": "It is the Sunna.", "reasons": "Jishumi presents the alternative; Ibn al-Jawzi's lexical survey cites 2:129, 2:231 and this verse; Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Kuranyolu adopt or report it."}, {"id": "4:113/q17/p3", "position": "Book and Wisdom together designate the Quran, with Wisdom as its nonlegal or clarifying content.", "reasons": "Alusi reads both qualities together; Kuranyolu reports the Quran's nonlegal knowledge for religious and worldly life."}, {"id": "4:113/q17/p4", "position": "It is a faculty to understand and apply revelation and judge well.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says it includes native cultivated judgment so the Prophet does not speak from whim; Kuranyolu reports a distinctive mental capacity, comparing 2:269."}, {"id": "4:113/q17/p5", "position": "It is prophethood.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur distinguishes Wisdom from the Quran and the further Sunna and unseen knowledge."}, {"id": "4:113/q17/p6", "position": "It is other divine teachings conveyed through revelation, beneficial in this world and the next.", "reasons": "Tabatabai rejects the Quran-rulings and Quran-Sunna identifications in favor of this broader category."}, {"id": "4:113/q17/p7", "position": "It is detailed rulings and manifestations of divine attributes, joined to action.", "reasons": "Qashani's inward account combines knowing and doing."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q18", "question": "What does ḥikma mean lexically and in other Quranic contexts?", "turns_on": "Lexical core versus context-specific Quranic usages.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q18/p1", "position": "Its root sense is restraint, and wisdom keeps its bearer from falsehood.", "reasons": "Ibn Faris gives ḥ-k-m as restraining a fool; Jarir's line asks Banu Hanifa to restrain fools; the horse's rein illustrates restraint; others define perfection of knowledge and action, or knowledge joined to action and justice."}, {"id": "4:113/q18/p2", "position": "In other verses it has several contextual senses: admonition, understanding, prophethood, Quran and Quranic sciences.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi lists admonition at 54:5, understanding at 6:89, 19:12, 21:79, 31:12, prophethood at 2:251 and 38:20, Quran at 16:125, and Quranic sciences at 2:269."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q19", "question": "What did God teach the Prophet that he had not known?", "turns_on": "Whether the teaching denotes law, unseen information, all divinely given knowledge, personal rank, or special inward knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q19/p1", "position": "Religious law, ordinances, and knowledge of lawful and unlawful conduct.", "reasons": "Muqatil says scripture and religion; Qatada adds this world and the next as proof against creation; Ibn Abbas and Muqatil are repeatedly cited for the law; Qaffal cites 42:52 for prior lack of Book and faith."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p2", "position": "Hidden events, thoughts, and otherwise unknown unseen matters.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baghawi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi name secrets within hearts; Bursevi says revelation conveyed unseen matters; Qaffal adds disclosure of hypocrites' schemes."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p3", "position": "Accounts of past and future peoples and events.", "reasons": "Tabari, Jishumi and Abu Sulayman state the historical scope; Qaffal extends it to future schemes."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p4", "position": "The Book and Wisdom themselves, including their secrets and realities.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qaffal give this explanation; Abu Hayyan cites 42:52; Alusi reports hidden mysteries."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p5", "position": "Everything previously unknown that God chose to disclose.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan prefers the inclusive reading over any one category; al-Bahr in Alusi likewise favors inclusion; Biqai names difficult, unseen and visible things of religion and worldly life."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p6", "position": "The Prophet's own worth, rank and servanthood before divine majesty.", "reasons": "Junayd says he was made to know his worth; Qushayri reports knowledge of God and His majesty, servanthood, and rank above others; Mawardi includes knowledge of noble worth."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p7", "position": "Knowledge of good and evil.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak is transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and Alusi."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p8", "position": "Hidden divine secrets or God's own knowledge disclosed in spiritual unveiling.", "reasons": "Sulami's anonymous gloss speaks of secrets known only through God; Qashani says the restored Prophet's heart knows through divine knowledge after annihilation."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p9", "position": "Knowledge beyond general Book and Wisdom: particular realities and judgment in disputes.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the context is concrete adjudication; the extra knowledge is distinct from general teachings and received directly, not through ordinary learning. He rejects listed Quran-ruling-Sunna identifications."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p10", "position": "The manners of servanthood and removal of confusion about knowing God.", "reasons": "Qushayri reports this distinct inward reading."}, {"id": "4:113/q19/p11", "position": "Knowledge of four stations: gnosis, expression, servanthood, and service.", "reasons": "Junayd says the Prophet received their greatest share."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q20", "question": "How was this teaching conveyed?", "turns_on": "Whether divine teaching is angelic revelation alone or includes direct inspiration and unveiling.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q20/p1", "position": "By revelation, with God as ultimate teacher and Gabriel as the messenger.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites 42:52–53 and 28:86; Tabatabai cites descent to the heart in 2:97 and 26:192–195 and further revelation texts 42:13, 4:163, 46:9 and 7:203; Samarrai says 53:2's 'strong in powers' identifies Gabriel, because ilham can also name lesser inspirations."}, {"id": "4:113/q20/p2", "position": "Through divine encounter, unveiling and direct spiritual knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti contrasts Muhammad's capacity to bear the Essence with Moses' bearing of the Attributes; Qashani describes unveiling, annihilation and restored existence."}, {"id": "4:113/q20/p3", "position": "Through both angelic revelation and direct inspiration cast into the heart.", "reasons": "Tabatabai distinguishes the two and cites reports, including the Holy Spirit supporting Prophet and Imam; he reads 42:52 as a guiding word cast to the Prophet and 21:73 as support of the Imam."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q21", "question": "How is 'you had not known' parsed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q21/p1", "position": "Taʿlamu is the predicate of takun; the negative construction is jussive.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi explain dropped final nūn ḍamma and wāw after two quiescent letters; Qurtubi calls taʿlam accusative as kāna's predicate."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q22", "question": "What is the great favor at the verse's end?", "turns_on": "Whether the culminating favor names one gift or the totality and force of divine benefaction.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q22/p1", "position": "Prophethood, especially the Prophet's universal mission and leadership.", "reasons": "Muqatil adds the Book; Damghani and Ibn al-Jawzi compare 17:87; Baydawi says nothing exceeds prophethood; Jishumi and Tabarsi add seal of prophets, master of messengers and intercession; Bursevi and Alusi add universal prophethood and supreme leadership."}, {"id": "4:113/q22/p2", "position": "All the singular gifts God gave the Prophet, beyond enumeration.", "reasons": "Jishumi dates favor from creation to mission; Abu Sulayman and Abu Hayyan include every special gift; Nasafi stresses what God taught and bestowed; Kuranyolu adds that humanity benefits from these qualities."}, {"id": "4:113/q22/p3", "position": "The knowledge God taught him.", "reasons": "Tabari calls historical and future knowledge favor; Razi and Study Quran infer knowledge's nobility from the repeated great-favor declaration; Qushayri says no gift rivals such knowledge. Bursevi cites the Prophet's prayer against useless knowledge and Muslim's report from Abu Hurayra that beneficial knowledge is among deeds whose reward continues after death."}, {"id": "4:113/q22/p4", "position": "Faith.", "reasons": "Tha'labi and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit Ibn Abbas's reading; Abu Hayyan also reports it."}, {"id": "4:113/q22/p5", "position": "The realized inward perfection bestowed on the Prophet.", "reasons": "Qashani attributes it to the practice bringing him to his attained state; Qushayri places the favor
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<chunk 103, part 1 of 0..5>>
 in divine pre-eternal regard."}, {"id": "4:113/q22/p6", "position": "A declaration of benefaction after the account of protection and teaching.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says this is the phrase's rhetorical force; Ibn Ashur observes its echo of the opening."}, {"id": "4:113/q22/p7", "position": "God Himself, understood as the Prophet's favor and mercy to the worlds.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes the saying about the spheres being created for the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q23", "question": "What does the word faḍl mean in this passage and Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "Lexical increase versus contextual benefaction or prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q23/p1", "position": "It may denote prophethood.", "reasons": "Damghani and Ibn al-Jawzi compare the Night Journey passage 17:87 with the concluding favor."}, {"id": "4:113/q23/p2", "position": "Its original sense is increase, and here it denotes benefaction or blessing.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi says figurative uses depend on context and compares the opening to 4:83, 12:38, 24:10 and 24:22."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q24", "question": "What does raḥma mean here and in other Quranic uses?", "turns_on": "The contextual sense of the term across the cited verses.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q24/p1", "position": "Here it can mean favor or blessing.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi compares 18:65 and also lists grace or favor at 28:46."}, {"id": "4:113/q24/p2", "position": "Elsewhere it can mean safety, deliverance, tenderness, forgiveness, relief, affection, or protection from wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites 39:38, 33:17, 57:27, 6:54, 2:178, 48:29 and 12:53 respectively."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q25", "question": "What does ḍalāl mean in Arabic and other Quranic uses?", "turns_on": "Which contextual shade of the root is in view.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q25/p1", "position": "Its base range includes confusion and departure from what is right.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi says ḍalāl and ḍalāla are synonymous, notes two verb forms, labels ḍalīl or muḍallal an erring person, and says aḍalla may mean bury the dead; Ibn al-Sikkit cites a missing camel and an unfound mosque or house; Jishumi describes turning from salvation to ruin."}, {"id": "4:113/q25/p2", "position": "Elsewhere it can signify misguidance, loss, misery, or futile nullification.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites 36:62 and 37:71 for misguidance; 12:8,95,97, 36:24, 40:25 for loss; 34:8 and 54:24 for misery; 18:103 and 47:1 for nullification."}, {"id": "4:113/q25/p3", "position": "It can mean deviation from a matter without unbelief.", "reasons": "Damghani compares David in 38:26."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q26", "question": "What does the verse teach about the Prophet's protection from error?", "turns_on": "Whether protection is explained by revelation, a distinct unfailing knowledge, or proper judicial reliance on appearances.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q26/p1", "position": "God guards him in religious conveyance and judgment through revelation and teaching.", "reasons": "Razi ties his future protection to scripture and the law he conveys; Ibn Kathir cites 42:52–53; Elmalili describes inward and outward protection; Kuranyolu covers conveying, teaching and applying religion; Study Quran calls the disclosure preservation of isma; Tabatabai denies a consequential sin or blameworthy approach."}, {"id": "4:113/q26/p2", "position": "The Prophet's apparent thought followed admissible evidence, so it involved no culpable bias or error.", "reasons": "Razi says revealed law itself requires outward evidence; Ibn Ashur's account says the opponents never gained confident intent; Elmalili says a judge cannot be liable for undisclosed contrary facts."}, {"id": "4:113/q26/p3", "position": "Infallibility is a special divinely given knowledge that cannot be overpowered by desire.", "reasons": "Tabatabai compares a settled disposition to courage or chastity but distinguishes ordinary beneficial knowledge, which can lapse as faculties compete; the Prophet's special knowledge dominates all other causes and prevents sin and error absolutely. He invokes 12:33, 42:52, 21:73 and reports on the Holy Spirit."}, {"id": "4:113/q26/p4", "position": "A favored prophet can stumble in a witnessed moment and then return after reproach to pre-eternal favor.", "reasons": "Sulami's anonymous voice compares 9:43."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q27", "question": "What practical response does the verse require of the Prophet and believers?", "turns_on": "The source's move from this protection to obedience, humility, and moral consequences.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q27/p1", "position": "The Prophet should thank God through obedience, adhere to revelation, and resist those diverting him.", "reasons": "Tabari says God will protect him in obedience while no one could save him if he followed their desire; the verse reminds him of his welfare and duty."}, {"id": "4:113/q27/p2", "position": "People should credit virtues and good deeds to divine favor, without self-admiration, while continuing to act.", "reasons": "Bursevi says even a lifetime of deeds cannot repay existence; Shah Shuja declines to prize fifty years of pilgrimage above one poor man's deed; al-Sa'di's verse attributes benefits to enabling grace."}, {"id": "4:113/q27/p3", "position": "Good and evil return to their actors.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites al-Sa'ib's poem and tales of a calf slaughterer and a charitable mother whose child was restored, illustrating consequences and mercy."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q28", "question": "What legal rules follow from the theft and advocacy case?", "turns_on": "The distinction between dishonest advocacy, impartial adjudication, and evidentiary limits.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q28/p1", "position": "One must not advocate a right for or against a person without knowing the facts.", "reasons": "Bursevi attributes the rule to al-Haddadi; Tabari grounds the prohibition in 4:105 and the duty not to aid sin."}, {"id": "4:113/q28/p2", "position": "A judge acting on apparent evidence is not liable for a hidden falsehood.", "reasons": "Elmalili states this legal implication; Razi says revealed law requires outward judgment."}, {"id": "4:113/q28/p3", "position": "A judge must treat Muslim and non-Muslim litigants without favoritism.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports al-Haddadi's rule."}, {"id": "4:113/q28/p4", "position": "Possession of stolen property alone does not establish that its possessor stole it.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports al-Haddadi's evidentiary rule."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q29", "question": "What inward readings are offered for the Prophet's favor and teaching?", "turns_on": "The different spiritual objects of teaching: rank, divine reality, servanthood, and perfected travel.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q29/p1", "position": "Divine encounter and eternal favor disclose divine realities and the Prophet's perfected state.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti contrasts bearing the Essence and Attributes; Qushayri reports pre-eternal honor; Qashani speaks of latent perfection, annihilation, and restoration in divine knowledge."}, {"id": "4:113/q29/p2", "position": "The Prophet receives the fullest spiritual knowledge and rank.", "reasons": "Junayd divides knowledge into gnosis, expression, servanthood and service; Abu Yazid distinguishes explanatory knowledge and proof; Sahl ranks believers, scholars, and prophets by knowledge of God, His commands and His days; al-Jurayri contrasts scholars' outward, sages' inward, and elders' essential perception; another scheme gives four scholars different shares. Qushayri says all borrow the Prophet's light and those outside his banner miss nearness."}, {"id": "4:113/q29/p3", "position": "The Prophet learns servanthood, and human knowledge of God depends on obedience.", "reasons": "Qushayri reports manners of service, clarity about the Real, and knowledge of God's measure proportionate to following His command."}, {"id": "4:113/q29/p4", "position": "No worldly or spiritual obstacle diverted him from arrival.", "reasons": "Bursevi names both kinds of obstacle and prays for protection and union with holy souls."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q30", "question": "What rhetorical pattern in the passage reinforces its message?", "turns_on": "The repeated forms and deliberately unspecified objects.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q30/p1", "position": "The repeated terms and balanced forms echo misguidance, teaching, and favor.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan notices yudilluka/ma yudillun and allamaka/ta'lam, plus passage-wide travel and battle metaphors and changed complements; Ibn Ashur identifies the closing 'great favor' as an echo of the opening."}, {"id": "4:113/q30/p2", "position": "The objects of seeing and knowing remain unspecified, creating meaningful ambiguity.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan notes the indeterminacy of bima araka Allah and ma lam takun ta'lam and ellipses across the passage."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q31", "question": "How is a paused hamza eased according to the reading tradition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q31/p1", "position": "Hamza's pause follows the Uthmani spelling, using an Arabic-permitted eased form that matches the written shape.", "reasons": "Sulaim transmits Hamza's practice; al-Dani, Faris, Makki, Ibn Shurayh and al-Shatibi are cited. Ibn al-Jazari says 'without analogy' means without analogy detached from the codex and that grammar still constrains the form; eased hamza is represented by alif, ya or waw, while initial hamza remains alif."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q32", "question": "May a pause signal the vowel of the pronoun hāʾ?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun's vowel is stable enough to signal, and whether surrounding sounds make signaling heavy.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q32/p1", "position": "Rūm or ishām may signal the pronoun vowel without restriction.", "reasons": "Many performance authorities and Ibn Mujahid permit this; al-Dani records it and calls it more analogical since the pronoun is like a fixed inflection. The general paus

e rule includes stable ḍamma except transferred or epenthetic vowels."}, {"id": "4:113/q32/p2", "position": "Neither signal is permitted on the pronoun hāʾ.", "reasons": "Other authorities reason its vowel is incidental; the apparent view of al-Shatibi supports this; al-Dani records the view as sound."}, {"id": "4:113/q32/p3", "position": "It is barred after matching ḍamma, silent wāw, kasra, or silent yāʾ, but allowed elsewhere.", "reasons": "A group of precise authorities uses ease of pronunciation and clarification to distinguish contexts, citing examples such as minhu and hudahu."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q33", "question": "How does the verse relate to other statements about Book and Wisdom?", "turns_on": "The cited intertext for the paired gifts and the mode of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q33/p1", "position": "The revelation and teaching here are God's guiding light and unexpected mercy.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares 42:52–53 and 28:86; Tabatabai reads 42:52 as Spirit and guiding word."}, {"id": "4:113/q33/p2", "position": "Other Quran verses also pair the Book and Wisdom as gifts to prophets.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 2:129,151,231; 3:81,164; 4:54; 5:110; and 62:2."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q34", "question": "What other sense of qawl is discussed in lexical notes adjacent to this passage?", "turns_on": "The different lexical and contextual senses in the source's wider survey.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q34/p1", "position": "Qawl and kalām overlap in ordinary usage, though some restrict kalām to meaningful speech.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi notes maqūl for tongue and qawla/qawwāl for a frequent speaker; a reported view excludes uninformative 'stood, sat' from kalām; Arabic examples and two poems show qawl can mean think or suppose, and Abu Zakariyya describes its syntax."}, {"id": "4:113/q34/p2", "position": "Other Quranic contexts use qawl for scripture, testimony, prior decree, or punishment.", "reasons": "The survey cites 39:18, 14:27, 32:13 and 27:82."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q35", "question": "What biographical accounts illustrate divine care for the Prophet?", "turns_on": "The distinct biographical episodes given in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q35/p1", "position": "Khadija and Abu Talib supported him until their deaths in the same year, three years before the Hijra.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq says Khadija sustained his Islam and Abu Talib defended him."}, {"id": "4:113/q35/p2", "position": "After Abu Talib's death Quraysh abused him openly, yet he assured his daughter God would protect him.", "reasons": "Urwa recounts dirt thrown onto the Prophet, his daughter washing it away in tears, and his reassurance."}, {"id": "4:113/q35/p3", "position": "He traveled alone to al-Taif seeking Thaqif's protection and acceptance of God's message.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq places the journey after Abu Talib's death and increased abuse."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q01", "question": "What prompted the question or revelation?", "turns_on": "Which occasion report fits the broad wording and the preceding carrion prohibition.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q01/p1", "position": "ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd al-Khayl asked about dogs and falcons catching prey, some dying before slaughter.", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. Jubayr supplies the two hunters; reports vary on prey species and number/names of dogs. Al-Baghawī calls this the sounder occasion. Al-Biqāʿī links their concern to carrion in 5:3. Al-Māwardī gives five dog names: al-Mukhtalis, Ghallāb, al-Ghānim, Sahlīb and al-Mutaʿāṭī; al-Qurṭubī instead lists Ṣalhab, Ghallāb, al-Mukhtalis, al-Mutanaʿis and an uncertain Akhṭab or Waththāb, while al-Ṭabrisī reports six dogs. Zayd is also called Ibn al-Muhalhil."}, {"id": "5:4/q01/p2", "position": "Dogs were ordered killed after Gabriel refused entry; people asked what of them was lawful.", "reasons": "Abū Rāfiʿ reports the puppy, Gabriel's refusal, the Medina/al-ʿAwālī order and the people's question; al-Ḥākim authenticated his report. ʿIkrima names ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, Saʿd ibn Khaythama and ʿUwaymir ibn Sāʿida; Muḥammad b. Kaʿb reports the same occasion more generally. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī questions the story's coherence."}, {"id": "5:4/q01/p3", "position": "ʿAdī alone asked about dog hunting and revelation followed the Prophet's initial silence.", "reasons": "ʿĀmir and al-Shaʿbī report the Prophet awaited an answer."}, {"id": "5:4/q01/p4", "position": "The question can be an anticipated or recurring question about food rather than one historical event.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr appeals to Qurʾānic present-tense يسألونك; Elmalılı also permits a general possible question. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats occasion reports as imperfect applications of the general wording."}, {"id": "5:4/q01/p5", "position": "People asked whether trained hunters counted among the predators prohibited in 5:3.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu ties the question to the prior prohibition of torn prey."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q02", "question": "What did the question ask about?", "turns_on": "Whether the question is comprehensive or specifically about game or dogs.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q02/p1", "position": "It asks which foods and meals are lawful after the prohibitions.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān connect it to the previous catalogue of forbidden food; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows an actual or anticipated request for a comprehensive account."}, {"id": "5:4/q02/p2", "position": "It asks specifically about game and slaughtered animals.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī report this narrower scope; Abū Ḥayyān says the answer expands beyond it."}, {"id": "5:4/q02/p3", "position": "It asks about uses of dogs ordered killed.", "reasons": "Abū Rāfiʿ reports this wording; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says 'this kind' denotes dogs and suggests the verse gives a broader criterion."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q03", "question": "How is ماذا parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether ذا is relative, predicative, or extra.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q03/p1", "position": "ماذا is one interrogative noun, with أحل as its predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān offer this equivalent parse."}, {"id": "5:4/q03/p2", "position": "ما is the interrogative subject and ذا a relative or predicate; أحل describes it.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī and others give this analysis; the relative ذا means 'that which'."}, {"id": "5:4/q03/p3", "position": "ذا is superfluous, so ما alone is the subject of أحل.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash cites ماذا بال نسوتكم: replacing it with ما الذي makes the poetic clause ill formed; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī also mention an extra ذا."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q04", "question": "Why is the question phrased in the third person?", "turns_on": "Whether لهم is indirect wording or direct quotation.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q04/p1", "position": "The third person follows يسألونك and reports the situation indirectly.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn note that لنا would quote the speakers directly; al-Rāzī objects to treating لهم as their verbatim words."}, {"id": "5:4/q04/p2", "position": "It is a verbatim question understood through an implicit verb of saying.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī invokes the question's sense of speech; al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān object that questioners would have said 'for us'."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q05", "question": "How does the interrogative clause follow يسألونك?", "turns_on": "Whether asking governs the interrogative directly or through implied speech.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q05/p1", "position": "The interrogative suspends the verb's action and serves as its clause complement without an omitted speech verb.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān compares 68:40; al-Samīn says asking leads to knowledge and can take an interrogative complement."}, {"id": "5:4/q05/p2", "position": "The question implies saying, or an omitted saying verb introduces the clause.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī give this account; al-Ālūsī rejects Abū Ḥayyān's objection."}, {"id": "5:4/q05/p3", "position": "An omitted noun such as 'the answer to what is lawful' supplies the object.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this grammatical alternative."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q06", "question": "Why is the answer verbal although the question is nominal?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbal answer follows meaning, an elided verb, or a rhetorical change.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q06/p1", "position": "The answer matches the question's meaning, not its nominal form.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn explain the verbal response this way; Ibn al-Muraḥḥal proposes a purposeful change of form."}, {"id": "5:4/q06/p2", "position": "An omitted verb should be understood before the answer.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī and al-Suyūṭī use this verse as an example of a full verbal answer that reveals the elided verb in shorter answers."}, {"id": "5:4/q06/p3", "position": "The different form is a deliberate rhetorical answer.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Muraḥḥal compares the reply about lunar phases in 2:189; al-Zarkashī questions the analysis."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q07", "question": "What are الطيبات?", "turns_on": "Whether goodness denotes legal permission, natural pleasantness, slaughter, or freedom from harm.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q07/p1", "position": "All lawful things, whether pleasant to eat or not.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Mujāhid's successors, al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās, Mālik and others gloss it as licit provision; al-Wāḥidī prefers its breadth. Al-Māwardī says legal goodness may be analogical to pleasantness. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats permission as a practical sign of goodness."}, {"id": "5:4/q07/p2", "position": "Pleasant, clean foods that sound human nature finds wholesome.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, Elmalılı and others cite 7:157's contrast with خبائث. They use cultivated taste rather than necessity-driven appetite; Ibn ʿĀshūr objects that local taste cannot govern a universal law, citing the Prophet's distaste for but permission of monitor lizard.

{"id": "5:4/q08", "question": "What food-law principle follows from الطيبات?", "turns_on": "Whether general permission is limited by taste, text, or particular reports.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q08/p1", "position": "Food and earthly benefits are presumed lawful until evidence forbids them, while foul or harmful things are excluded.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuranyolu invoke 2:29, 7:157 and 7:32; Asad limits Qurʾānic prohibitions to injury. This corrects pagan bans on baḥīra, sāʾiba, waṣīla and ḥām."}, {"id": "5:4/q08/p2", "position": "Palatability of Arabs, especially cultivated urban Hijazis, controls unlisted animal foods.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites lizards, jerboas and rabbits; Muḥammad al-Kākī describes comparison with Hijazi tastes. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects making a regional custom universal, citing Khālid's monitor lizard report."}, {"id": "5:4/q08/p3", "position": "Horse meat is lawful as pleasant food.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī applies the general permission; Abū Ḥanīfa disagrees."}, {"id": "5:4/q08/p4", "position": "Horse meat is impermissible.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥanīfa's contrary ruling is reported by al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr."}, {"id": "5:4/q08/p5", "position": "Domestic donkey meat is lawful under the general permission.", "reasons": "Mālik and Bishr al-Marīsī are reported so; al-Rāzī invokes the Prophet's Khaybar prohibition against them."}, {"id": "5:4/q08/p6", "position": "Domestic donkey meat is forbidden by the Khaybar report.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī takes the Prophet's prohibition to specify the general verse."}, {"id": "5:4/q08/p7", "position": "Specific things such as therapeutic urine or edible clay are not wholesome.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports al-Zuhrī excluding urine as treatment and Mālik excluding sale of clay eaten by people."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q09", "question": "What slaughter by People of the Book is permitted?", "turns_on": "Whether scripturalist slaughter is covered when another name is pronounced.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q09/p1", "position": "Their slaughter is lawful, even if they invoke Christ or prepare a church offering.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports the majority, al-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhrī and Makḥūl; they read the permission for scripturalists' food broadly and take prohibitions on idolatrous naming as directed at polytheists. Al-Thaʿlabī distinguishes Jews, Christians and pre-mission adherents from later converts in one report."}, {"id": "5:4/q09/p2", "position": "Slaughter naming Christ is forbidden or disliked, especially when heard.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar cites 6:121; al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥārith al-ʿAklī distinguish hearing another name from absence."}, {"id": "5:4/q09/p3", "position": "Only a Muslim may slaughter a Muslim ritual sacrifice.", "reasons": "ʿAlī distinguishes the special offering from ordinary food."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q10", "question": "How is وما علمتم connected syntactically to the answer?", "turns_on": "Whether ما is coordinated, conditional, or a new relative construction.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q10/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with الطيبات and implies 'the game or catch of what you trained'.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and others infer the omission from فكلوا; al-Qurṭubī says eating the predators themselves is not intended."}, {"id": "5:4/q10/p2", "position": "ما is conditional and فكلوا is its answer, with no implied catch needed.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefer avoiding ellipsis; al-Ālūsī says permissions attach to actions."}, {"id": "5:4/q10/p3", "position": "ما is a relative subject whose predicate is فكلوا, with فاء by analogy with a condition.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī report this less apparent parse."}, {"id": "5:4/q10/p4", "position": "The clause starts a new sentence, and فكلوا supplies its result.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī report this explanation without requiring coordination with الطيبات."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q11", "question": "What does الجوارح mean and why are they so named?", "turns_on": "Whether the name comes from earning prey or wounding it.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q11/p1", "position": "Hunting creatures called earners or catchers because they procure prey for their owners.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī and many later authors use the root for acquisition; 6:60 and 45:21, al-Aʿshā's line, and a family's provider substantiate the sense. The singular is جارحة."}, {"id": "5:4/q11/p2", "position": "They are predators named for wounding prey.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this etymology; al-Rāzī links it to requiring a bleeding wound. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī call it weak; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Biqāʿī allow it alongside earning."}, {"id": "5:4/q11/p3", "position": "The word denotes trained dogs.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba and Muqātil gloss it this way in context; other authorities extend it to birds and beasts."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q12", "question": "Which hunting animals are covered?", "turns_on": "Whether jawāriḥ includes birds and beasts despite مُكَلِّبِينَ.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q12/p1", "position": "Every trainable hunting beast and bird, including dogs, cheetahs, falcons and hawks.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and most commentators cite general wording; al-Ṭabarī prefers it. {"id": "5:4/q13", "question": "What does مكلبين mean and why use this term?", "turns_on": "Whether the word denotes training, ownership, eagerness, or a broad use of dog.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q13/p1", "position": "Skilled trainers who set hunting animals on prey; dogs name the craft because they are its commonest subjects.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabarī, al-Kashshāf and others say the term qualifies the handlers and stresses expertise. {"id": "5:4/q14", "question": "What is the grammatical role of مكلبين?", "turns_on": "Whether the circumstance qualifies people or animals.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q14/p1", "position": "It is an accusative circumstantial qualifier of the people who trained the hunters.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Naḥḥās, al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī and others emphasize human skill. Al-Kashshāf says it is not redundant with عَلَّمْتُم."}, {"id": "5:4/q14/p2", "position": "It qualifies the hunting animals themselves as trained.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this third analysis; Ibn Kathīr says it can describe the animals rather than the human subject."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q15", "question": "What variant readings occur here?", "turns_on": "Active versus passive verb and heavy versus light lām.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q15/p1", "position": "مُكْلِبِينَ has a light lām, from أكلب; it can mean trainers or owners of many dogs.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd, al-Ḥasan, Abū Zurayn and others are cited; Form IV may overlap with doubled Form II, though al-Zajjāj distinguishes trainer from dog owner."}, {"id": "5:4/q15/p2", "position": "عُلِّمْتُم is passive, referring to the instruction people received about hunting.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya transmit this reading; al-Samīn notes that God is the understood agent."}, {"id": "5:4/q15/p3", "position": "عَلَّمْتُم is active and مُكَلِّبِينَ has doubled lām.", "reasons": "Most readers use these forms; Jishumī and al-Qurṭubī explain the ordinary subject and intensive trainer."}]}

{"id": "5:4/q17", "question": "How many successful trials establish training?", "turns_on": "Whether custom or one, two, or three demonstrations fixes the threshold.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q17/p1", "position": "Three successes are required.", "reasons": "Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan require three demonstrations; some allow the third catch, others the fourth."}, {"id": "5:4/q17/p2", "position": "No fixed number; repeated behavior or hunters' custom establishes it.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa in a principal report, al-Biqāʿī and others appeal to habitual obedience; al-Biqāʿī notes no text or consensus fixes a count."}, {"id": "5:4/q17/p3", "position": "One successful hunt suffices.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and some jurists count the first success, making the second catch edible in one formulation."}, {"id": "5:4/q17/p4", "position": "Two successes suffice.", "reasons": "Another Abū Ḥanīfa report and Aḥmad require two repetitions."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q18", "question": "How is من in مما علمكم الله understood?", "turns_on": "Whether مِن expresses source or comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q18/p1", "position": "It is partitive or marks the source/cause of human training knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī insists من has meaning and rejects substituting كاف; Ibn ʿAṭiyya permits a portion or origin, and al-Ālūsī cause or portion."}, {"id": "5:4/q18/p2", "position": "It means 'as God taught you'.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī gives this paraphrase; al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭabrisī reject equating partitive من with comparative كاف."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q19", "question": "How is تعلمونهن construed?", "turns_on": "Which clause teaching modifies.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q19/p1", "position": "It is a second circumstantial clause emphasizing the handlers' teaching.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān and others attach it to the people or the hidden pronoun in مكلبين; al-Samīn reports a nested حال."}, {"id": "5:4/q19/p2", "position": "It cannot directly qualify الجوارح across مكلبين.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn rejects that separation; Abū al-Baqāʾ also objects to two circumstantials governed by one verb."}, {"id": "5:4/q19/p3", "position": "It begins an independent sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Samīn permit this, especially if ما is not conditional."}, {"id": "5:4/q19/p4", "position": "It is parenthetical between condition and answer.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this if ما is conditional or relative with فكلوا as predicate."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q20", "question": "May trained hunters be kept, trained, or sold?", "turns_on": "Which benefits justify keeping dogs after the killing order.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q20/p1", "position": "Useful hunting dogs and other service dogs may be kept; training and sale are permitted.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī exempt hunting, livestock and field dogs from the earlier killing order; al-Ālūsī includes guard dogs by analogy and permits useful corrective training. Elmalılı permits buying and selling."}, {"id": "5:4/q20/p2", "position": "Unneeded dogs are prohibited or reduce daily reward by one or two qīrāṭs.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayra give different deductions; explanations include barking at guests, keeping angels away and impurity. Al-Qurṭubī proposes differences by dog harm or place. Ibn ʿUmar reports two qīrāṭs, Abū Hurayra one in another version; al-Qurṭubī relates the difference to harm or city."}, {"id": "5:4/q20/p3", "position": "Harmful or rabid dogs should be killed, harmless useful dogs spared.", "reasons": "Reports from the dog-killing occasion and al-Thaʿlabī draw the distinction; the solid-black dog is singled out in some reports."}, {"id": "5:4/q20/p4", "position": "A dog may protect a house as well as livestock or crops.", "reasons": "Some jurists extend the benefit rule to rural houses; Mālik confines the livestock dog to accompanying animals to pasture."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q21", "question": "Can a wholly black dog be used for hunting?", "turns_on": "Whether the black-dog reports restrict the general wording.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q21/p1", "position": "No, or it is disliked, because the black dog is called a devil and ordered killed.", "reasons": "Aḥmad, Isḥāq, some literalists, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and al-Nakhaʿī object; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the prayer-crossing proof weak and figurative."}, {"id": "5:4/q21/p2", "position": "Yes, any trained dog is covered by the verse's general wording.", "reasons": "Jurists of Medina and Kufa and the majority permit it; Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the unrestricted text."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q22", "question": "Does the trainer's religion affect the catch?", "turns_on": "Whether non-Muslim training affects the catch.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q22/p1", "position": "A Magian-trained dog or bird is disfavored or its catch unlawful even if a Muslim invokes God.", "reasons": "Jābir, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, al-Thawrī and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported so; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects Ibn ʿAbbās's premise that only Muslims receive God-given training."}, {"id": "5:4/q22/p2", "position": "A Muslim may use a dog trained or owned by a non-Muslim, even a Magian.", "reasons": "Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compare the trained animal to a borrowed knife; God's teaching is not exclusive to Muslims."}, {"id": "5:4/q22/p3", "position": "A Jewish or Christian trainer's dog is disfavored.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan bases his dislike on the verse's address to believers."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q23", "question": "Whose own hunting is lawful?", "turns_on": "Whether hunting follows slaughter rules and who qualifies as hunter.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q23/p1", "position": "A Muslim or scripturalist may hunt, but a Magian's game is generally forbidden.", "reasons": "The majority treats hunting as a kind of ritual slaughter; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this principle. {"id": "5:4/q24", "question": "What makes a killed catch lawful without ordinary slaughter?", "turns_on": "Whether a trained hunter's action counts as slaughter.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q24/p1", "position": "A released, trained hunter's wound substitutes for slaughter when its owner invoked God; live prey must be slaughtered.", "reasons": "The Prophet's reports to ʿAdī and Abū Thaʿlaba distinguish trained from untrained animals; al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, Elmalılı and others extend the rule to trained beasts, birds and piercing arrows. {"id": "5:4/q25", "question": "What if caught prey remains alive or dies before slaughter?", "turns_on": "Whether live prey could be slaughtered before death.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q25/p1", "position": "Prey found alive must be slaughtered if the hunter can do so; neglect makes it unlawful.", "reasons": "The Prophet's ʿAdī report commands slaughter of live prey; al-Qurṭubī says an accessible animal dying while the hunter negligently delays is not edible, though reaching for a knife already present is excused. Khadīj blood-flow report, al-Muzanī's arrow analogy, legal specification and retained blood."}, {"id": "5:4/q26/p2", "position": "Yes; the general permission covers a trained animal's catch even if its impact kills without bloodshed.", "reasons": "Some Shāfiʿī authorities, al-Nawawī and al-Rāfiʿī are reported so; al-Wāḥidī says owner-directed holding, not wounding, is decisive. Ibn Kathīr contests attributing a firm position to al-Shāfiʿī."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q27", "question": "What if the hunting animal ate part of the prey?", "turns_on": "Whether eating proves the animal caught for itself and how contrary reports are reconciled.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q27/p1", "position": "The prey is unlawful unless found alive and slaughtered; eating shows it held the prey for itself.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, the sound ʿAdī report, al-Ṭabarī, the predominant Shāfiʿī view and many authorities apply the words 'for you' strictly. Some distinguish a trained bird; al-Ṭabarī extends the bar to every predator."}, {"id": "5:4/q27/p2", "position": "The uneaten remainder remains lawful, even if little remains.", "reasons": "Salmān, Saʿd, Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayra report allowances of two-thirds eaten or only a morsel left. Mālik, al-Layth and Ibn ʿĀshūr accept owner-directed catch despite appetite. Abū Thaʿlaba's report permits dog-eaten game; al-Qurṭubī favors legal permission with the restrictive report as caution. Al-Qurṭubī deems an ʿAdī permission version unsound, accepts Abū Thaʿlaba's report as permission and treats the ʿAdī prohibition as caution; Ibn Kathīr rates two Abū Thaʿlaba chains good, while al-Ṭabarī criticizes an alleged Salmān-to-Prophet chain because Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib's hearing is unproven."}, {"id": "5:4/q27/p3", "position": "Dogs and land beasts must abstain, but predatory birds may eat.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and others say dogs can be beaten into abstention whereas hawks cannot; Ibn Kathīr notes ʿAdī's falcon wording omits the dog's condition."}, {"id": "5:4/q27/p4", "position": "A bird that eats also invalidates its catch.", "reasons": "ʿAlī, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrima and some reports from al-Shaʿbī and ʿAṭāʾ apply the same 'for itself' test to falcons."}, {"id": "5:4/q27/p5", "position": "If the dog ate only after first holding prey for its owner and becoming hungry, the remainder is lawful.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr prefers this reconciliation of contrary reports; some Shāfiʿī colleagues allow a hungry dog's lapse."}, {"id": "5:4/q27/p6", "position": "The reports conflict; the permissive report abrogates the restrictive one.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUmar proposes chronology from the more explicit Abū Thaʿlaba answer; al-Qurṭubī objects that the dates are unknown and prefers reconciliation."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q28", "question": "Does drinking blood count as eating from prey?", "turns_on": "Whether drinking blood counts as eating.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q28/p1", "position": "No; the prey remains lawful.", "reasons": "Most jurists and ʿAṭāʾ distinguish drinking blood from eating flesh."}, {"id": "5:4/q28/p2", "position": "Yes, or the prey is disliked.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī and Sufyān al-Thawrī disapprove; Abū Ḥayyān says the apparent rule equates it with eating."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q29", "question": "What if the catch disappears before it is found dead?", "turns_on": "Whether the fatal cause remains certain after disappearance.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q29/p1", "position": "Unseen dead prey is not eaten because another cause of death is possible.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites the instruction to eat a witnessed kill and leave what disappeared; al-Qurṭubī cites Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Thawrī and al-Shāfiʿī. The words iṣmāʾ and inmāʾ distinguish witnessed and lost quarry, illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays."}, {"id": "5:4/q29/p2", "position": "It may be eaten if a sole mortal wound or arrow mark proves the hunter's cause, even after a day or three.", "reasons": "Reports from Abū Thaʿlaba, al-Awzāʿī, Ashhab and others allow delayed recovery without another wound or drowning; Abū ʿUmar infers a similar Mālik position. Stench causes dislike or danger."}, {"id": "5:4/q29/p3", "position": "An unseen arrow kill is allowed, but an unseen dog kill is barred.", "reasons": "A reported position says an arrow has one clear mechanism whereas a dog can kill several ways."}, {"id": "5:4/q29/p4", "position": "Any unseen prey is allowed if the hunter's arrow or dog killed it.", "reasons": "One of al-Qurṭubī's reported positions allows both forms."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q30", "question": "What confirms the cause of death for arrow or dog game?", "turns_on": "Whether a fatal mark establishes cause over water or a rival hunter.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q30/p1", "position": "A penetrating arrow or certain trained-hunter wound suffices; a flat-side blow or drowning does not.", "reasons": "The ʿAdī report distinguishes a piercing miʿrāḍ from its blunt side, and excludes water or another arrow mark. Al-Qurṭubī demands certainty about the fatal cause. The same reports warn against a second uninvoked dog, an unknown arrow mark, and a body found in water."}, {"id": "5:4/q30/p2", "position": "A lost catch can still be eaten if a sole fatal mark identifies the hunter's weapon.", "reasons": "Abū Thaʿlaba's and other reports permit delayed retrieval where no rival cause appears; al-Qurṭubī juxtaposes the contrary visible-kill instruction."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q31", "question": "What if another dog joins the hunt?", "turns_on": "Whether an unknown dog may have killed the prey.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q31/p1", "position": "Do not eat if an unnamed or untrained dog may have killed the prey.", "reasons": "The Prophet's ʿAdī report and later authorities stress uncertainty of the killer and that God's name was invoked only over the hunter's own dog; al-Qurṭubī presumes a stray joined on its own."}, {"id": "5:4/q31/p2", "position": "If another hunter sent a dog, the hunters share the catch; if the first dog inflicted the fatal wound, its owner takes it.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes jointly caused catches from a preexisting mortal wound."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q32", "question": "Must the hunter release the animal intentionally?", "turns_on": "Whether the hunt belongs to the owner's dispatch.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q32/p1", "position": "Yes; self-started hunting is excluded because it was not sent for the owner.", "reasons": "The majority, Rabīʿa, Abū Ḥanīfa, Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī require release or urging; al-Qurṭubī grounds it in intention, and Ibn ʿĀshūr allows an understood command."}, {"id": "5:4/q32/p2", "position": "Taking the animal out to hunt is enough even if it starts the chase itself.", "reasons": "ʿAlī, al-Awzāʿī and ʿAṭāʾ are reported to allow this."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q33", "question": "What does من in مما أمسكن express?", "turns_on": "Whether مِن is partitive, extra, or relevant to a partially eaten catch.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q33/p1", "position": "It is partitive, either idiomatic with eating or because only edible parts of prey are eaten.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes flesh from blood and offal; al-Bursawī names hides and bones. Ibn ʿĀshūr says ordinary partitive usage does not forbid the whole catch; al-Qurṭubī rejects the offal rationale as unnatural."}, {"id": "5:4/q33/p2", "position": "It is an extra or emphatic particle: eat what they caught.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and some Basrans compare 2:271, 24:43 and 6:141; al-Ṭabarī and other grammarians object that من contributes meaning or is not extra in an affirmative statement."}, {"id": "5:4/q33/p3", "position": "It permits eating what remains after an animal has eaten.", "reasons": "Some Maliki colleagues infer this; Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects using the common من for that inference."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q34", "question": "What does عليكم mean in أمسكن عليكم?", "turns_on": "Whether على denotes benefit or control.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q34/p1", "position": "It means for the hunter's benefit or on the hunter's behalf.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites ʿAlqama's poem and 33:37 for causal على; al-Samīn calls the literal spatial relation figurative."}, {"id": "5:4/q34/p2", "position": "It marks the prey as held under the hunter's direction rather than for the animal.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and many jurists derive the owner-directed condition from it."}]}
{"id": "5:4/q35", "question": "To what does عليه refer, and when is God's name mentioned?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun denotes the hunter, live prey, or eating.", "positions": [{"id": "5:4/q35/p1", "position": "It refers to the released hunter or its dispatch; invoke God at release.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn Kathīr and most jurists cite the Prophet's command to name God when sending a dog or arrow."}, {"id": "5:4/q35/p2", "position": "It refers to eating; invoke God over the meal.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān prefer this and cite the Prophet's meal instruction; al-Ālūsī deems it less likely."}, {"id": "5:4/q35/p3", "position": "It refers to prey reached alive; name God when slaughtering it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī and others offer this antecedent; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the compact wording covers release and slaughter."}]}
